title: Dead, live, wind and snow loads: what a structure must carry
examples: What is the difference between dead load and live load?
How do engineers combine loads with safety factors?
What loads act on a building?

supports.ask: Why are loads multiplied by safety factors?

explain.say: Every building carries far more than you can see. A floor in a Mumbai flat must hold its own concrete and tiles, and also you, your sofa and a room full of friends. Engineers sort all of this into types of load. Let us load one six metre floor beam and see.

draw.text: Dead, live, wind and snow loads: what a structure must carry

supports.ask: Why are loads multiplied by safety factors?

explain.say: Look at the first spread load, four kilonewtons per metre. That is dead load: the permanent weight of the structure itself, the slab, the beam and the floor finish. It never leaves. Can you name one dead load in the room around you?

supports.ask: Why are loads multiplied by safety factors?

draw.text: Dead load is worked out from sizes and unit weights of materials.

explain.say: Now the second load, three kilonewtons per metre. That is live load, also called imposed load: people, furniture, stored goods. It comes and goes, so codes give a safe value for each use, about two kilonewtons per square metre for homes and far more for library stacks. Together, each support pushes up twenty one kilonewtons.

supports.ask: Why are loads multiplied by safety factors?

explain.say: Now step outside the building. Wind pushes sideways on the walls and can even suck upwards on a roof, while snow sits on top, heavy in Canada or northern Japan and zero in Chennai. Wind is why a tall tower must be stiff sideways, not just strong downwards. Which arrow on the board is the only sideways one?

forces.label: Wind
forces.ask: How does wind load act on a building?

draw.text: Wind and snow loads come from maps of local climate in the codes.

explain.say: Yes, the wind! Engineers never just add loads. They multiply each by a safety factor first: one point three five times dead plus one point five times live gives nine point nine kilonewtons per metre here, and each support must take twenty nine point seven. Exam tip: always list loads by type first, then combine them.

loads.label: Design 9.9 kN/m
loads.ask: Why are loads multiplied by safety factors?

faq.a: Dead load is the permanent weight of the structure and everything fixed to it: slabs, beams, walls, finishes and services. It is found from the sizes and unit weights of the materials, such as about 25 kilonewtons per cubic metre for reinforced concrete.

Live load, or imposed load, is the weight that comes and goes: people, furniture, vehicles and stored goods. Codes give values for each use, for example about 2 kilonewtons per square metre for homes.
asks: What is a live load in a building?

faq.q: How does wind load act on a building?
faq.a: Wind pushes on the side facing it and sucks on the far side and often on the roof. The pressure grows with the square of the wind speed, so tall buildings and exposed sites get the biggest wind loads.

faq.q: Why are loads multiplied by safety factors?
faq.a: Real loads can be bigger than expected and materials weaker. Multiplying loads by factors like 1.35 for dead and 1.5 for live gives a design load the structure must survive with a margin.
Snow load is the weight of snow lying on a roof. It depends on the local climate and the roof shape, and in snowy regions it can reach several kilonewtons per square metre.
asks: How heavy is snow on a roof?

facts: Eurocode EN 1990 uses partial factors of 1.35 on permanent actions and 1.5 on variable actions in the usual strength combination.
Reinforced concrete weighs about 25 kilonewtons per cubic metre.
India's code IS 875 sets design loads for buildings, with Part 3 covering wind.

quiz.say: A beam carries a dead load of 6 kilonewtons per metre and a live load of 4. What is the design load using 1.35 times dead plus 1.5 times live?
quiz.show: A beam carries dead 6 kN/m and live 4 kN/m. Design load with 1.35G + 1.5Q?
quiz.why: 1.35 × 6 = 8.1 and 1.5 × 4 = 6, so the design load is 14.1 kilonewtons per metre.

wrong.0: That is just the loads added with no safety factors.
wrong.2: That uses 1.5 on both loads; dead load takes 1.35.
